description: We are Seeklon Valley, a team of three computer science students from Epitech : Deniz, Thomas and Robin, participating in the Paris local event. While not space technology specialists, we are driven by curiosity and problem-solving, bringing hands-on skills in software development, AI/ML, and data analysis to tackle this challenge. Our team is already complete.
summary:
IGNIS turns microgravity combustion research into an interactive 3D fire-safety workbench. Users explore spacecraft-inspired interiors, inspect equipment and materials, and visualize where heat and smoke could spread after an assumed electrical incident.

We combine traceable NASA findings from BASS/BASS-II, Saffire and SAME with physics-based simulations and a compact 3D neural network. The dashboard summarizes research, ranks relevant evidence against scenario conditions, and supports cited interpretations. Users can compare learned predictions with the FDS simulation reference and inspect errors over time.

Our verified six-family benchmark contains 384 simulated scenarios across 48 layouts. On 84 held-out microgravity scenarios, retraining improved heat and smoke F1 scores to 48.5% and 54.3%. NASA observations inform the evidence layer; synthetic FDS outputs supply the spatial training labels.

IGNIS demonstrates how accessible research, spatial visualization and machine learning can support future spacecraft fire-safety studies. It is a research proof of concept, with explicit uncertainty and limitations.
details:
Spacecraft fire safety depends on the interaction between materials, equipment placement, atmosphere and ventilation. In microgravity, reduced buoyancy changes combustion and smoke transport, making familiar Earth-based intuition insufficient. NASA has investigated these phenomena for decades, but understanding how findings relate to a particular scenario requires comparing experiments with different conditions, measurements and limitations.

IGNIS addresses this challenge through an evidence explorer and an interactive 3D simulation and machine-learning workbench.

Making NASA research accessible

We imported experimental inventories from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository for BASS, BASS-II and Saffire-I. We also curated 22 findings across 13 NASA sources covering combustion, electrical ignition mechanisms, overheating and smoke detection.

The dashboard ranks findings using explicit criteria, including material, mechanism, gravity, oxygen, pressure and available observations. It preserves source links, document locations, missing information and contradictory findings. Related publications are identified so that a presentation and its underlying paper are not treated as independent experiments.

Codex-assisted interpretation explains the relevance and limitations of selected evidence using archived facts and citations. As a concrete data-processing contribution, we extracted 211 admissible fan-calibration pairs from the BASS-II workbook and documented their units, exclusions and variability between sessions.

Exploring consequences in 3D

Users inspect spacecraft-inspired compartments containing equipment, material annotations, electrical source locations and ventilation openings. Original Blender scenes and GLB exports establish a workflow for connecting visual geometry with explicit physical metadata. Detailed rendering remains distinct from the simplified geometry used for computation.

The current spatial demonstration covers six compartment families: laboratory, junction node, service compartment, cargo, capsule-inspired interior and central racks. Users can move inside a scene, explore its timeline, toggle heat and smoke, and compare machine-learning predictions with the FDS reference and an error view.

Electrical incidents are represented through prescribed source scenarios, including overheating, arcing equivalents, flaming, smoldering and battery equivalents. These scenarios explore conditional consequences; they do not establish the probability that a component will fail or ignite.

Training and evaluating the spatial model

We generated a verified benchmark of 384 FDS scenarios across 48 layouts, partitioned into 240 training, 48 validation and 96 test scenarios. Layouts are separated between partitions.

An unchanged PyTorch 3D U-Net, containing 379,046 parameters, receives 54 input channels describing geometry, materials, source conditions, boundary ventilation and time. It predicts two spatial classes at 1,536 sample locations: temperature exceeding ambient by 5°C, and soot concentration exceeding 10⁻⁶ kg/m³.

On the same 84 microgravity test scenarios, retraining increased heat F1 from 24.6% to 48.5% and smoke F1 from 27.6% to 54.3%, compared with the previous model after threshold recalibration. Checkpoints and thresholds were selected using validation data before test evaluation.

Training ran on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti with 12 GB VRAM. FDS simulations ran on CPU. The browser demonstration replays saved predictions; a separate Python interface supports fresh inference.

Originality, impact and limitations

IGNIS connects experimental evidence, spatial context and learned simulation results in one inspectable workflow. Its intended impact is to support research communication, education and early exploration of spacecraft layouts and fire scenarios.

NASA observations supply scientific context and documentary evidence. The spatial network learns from synthetic FDS outputs, not NASA experimental flame fields. Current results demonstrate a limited proof of concept on new layouts within known families. They do not establish flight readiness, universal generalization or calibrated ignition probabilities.

The implementation uses Python, FastAPI, PyTorch, React, TypeScript, Three.js, Blender and NIST FDS, with reproducible datasets, recorded provenance, automated tests and independent export verification.
